Rheumatoid Arthritis
Med-Surg III Professor Coccimiglio
By Lori Choi, Alessia Cipriano, Patricia Dabrowski, Uchenna Egbujor, Patricia Ebrahim, Maegan 
Lewis, Linda Tan

Risk Factors + Early Detection
Non-Modifiable Modifiable
● Genetics: 
presence of 
human leukocyte 
antigen (HLA)
● Sex: Women are 
2-3x more likely to 
develop
● Age: Peak onset is 
between 30-50 
years
● History: First 
degree relatives 
have 2-3x 
increased risk
● Cigarette smoking
● Chronic gum 
diseases  →
encourage 
citrullination
● Obesity 
● Job related 
exposures (silica, 
dust, asbestos, 
mineral oils)
● Chronic stress
Early Detection
● First 12 weeks is the “window of opportunity”
○ Critical time-frame to initiate 
DMARDs
● Clinical Signs
○ Symmetrical polyarthritis
○ Prolonged morning stiffness 
○ “Boggy” synovitis
○ Low grade fever, malaise, fatigue, rheumatoid 
nodules
● Diagnostic Workups
○ Serology: Anti-citrullinated protein, rheumatoid 
factor
○ Inflammatory markers: Elevated ESR and CRP
○ Imaging: MRI or high resolution musculoskeletal 
ultrasound
■ In the 12 week window, plain X-rays will 
appear normal

Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention Health Promotion
● Primary prevention focuses on 
removing environmental triggers
○ Quitting smoking
● Maintain good dental hygiene to 
prevent periodontitis 
● Limit environmental toxins
○ Respiratory protection
● Healthy weight maintenance
● Healthy habits to help preserve 
independence and minimize 
complications
● Low impact physical activity
● Usage of assistive devices with help 
of PT/OT
● Anti-inflammatory diet
● Cardiovascular risk reduction
● Bone density care

Clinical Manifestations
Signs and Symptoms
● Bilateral symmetrical joint swelling
○ Common targets include small joints such as 
the MCP and PIP joints
●  Pain that increases with rest and decreases with 
activity
● Morning stiffness, often lasting more than 1 hour
● Swan neck deformities, boutonniere deformities, 
ulnar deviation and ankylosis
● Subcutaneous nodules
● Articular cartilage, bone destruction and synovitis
● Low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy, fatigue, malaise, 
weight loss, scleral redness
● Multisystem involvement
○ Cardiovascular and pulmonary involvement
Lab Values
● Positive rheumatoid factor (RF) antibody, positive 
Antinuclear Antibody (ANA) titer
● Elevated WBCs, ESR, CRP

Diagnostic Tests & Nursing Responsibilities
Diagnostic Tests
• Physical Exam
• Blood Tests:
● Inflammatory Markers: CRP (<1.0 mg/L), ESR 
(<15 mm/hr ♂, <20 mm/hr ♀)
● Autoantibodies (Positive): RF (anti-Fc portion of 
IgG), ACPAs
• Imaging Tests:
● X-ray / MRI: Shows joint damage & deformities
• Arthrocentesis (Joint Aspiration):
Normal Joint: Clear, pale yellow, viscous. WBC <200, Neutrophils 
<25%
Inflammatory RA / Reactive: Translucent/opaque, 
yellow/cloudy, WBC 2,000–50,000, Neutrophils >50%
*~10% of RA patients are seronegative (no RF or ACPA)
*Confirm with physical findings, morning stiffness >1 hr, markers & 
imaging
Nursing Responsibilities
1. Inflammatory Tests (ESR / CRP)
● No NPO required
● Document recent NSAIDs / corticosteroids (can falsely 
lower markers)
2. Imaging Care
● Plain X-Ray: No prep, contrast, or fasting needed
● Contrast MRI: Verify eGFR (prevent NSF); 
metformin hold not required unless iodinated CT 
ordered
3. Arthrocentesis Precautions
● Verify coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT, platelets) to 
prevent hemarthrosis
● Contraindicated over active cellulitis/broken skin 
(septic arthritis risk)
● Screen for chlorhexidine, latex, and lidocaine allergies

Physical Findings

Medical Management
Pharmacological Therapy
● Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs 
(DMARDS)
○ Suppress the immune system
■ Methotrexate, 
Hydroxychloroquine, 
Sulfasalazine
● Biologic DMARDS, such as TNF inhibitors
○ Second-line; block specific 
inflammatory pathways
● Corticosteroids
○ Prednisone, methylprednisolone
● NSAIDS
● Corticosteroid injections
Other Management
● Arthrocentesis
○ Aspirates excess fluid from inflamed 
joint
● Total joint arthroplasty
● Physical and occupational therapy
● Routine labs
○ Anemia common in RA
○ Liver and kidney function
○ Neutropenia risk
● Cardiovascular screenings
● Bone density scans (DEXA scans)

Medication Management & Nursing Responsibilities
Medication Regimen
● Based upon clinical findings and PMH.
Managing Adverse Effects
● DMARDs: processed heavily by the liver.
○ Routine blood testing for liver and 
kidney function.
○ Monitor CBC for anemia.
○ Avoid alcohol.
● NSAIDs: gastric ulcers
○ COX-2 enzyme blockers present 
less gastric irritation but an 
increased risk for cardiovascular 
disease.
● Corticosteroids: weight gain
○ Lowest dose for the shortest time 
possible.
Key Priorities
● Address pain, sleep disturbances, fatigue, altered mood, and 
limited mobility.
● Educate patient with a new diagnosis to assist with self-
management and coping.
Diet & Lifestyle
● Consult dietician to assess and assist with food choices.
● Encourage a diet high in vitamins, protein, and iron to build & 
repair tissue.
● Suggest a mediterranean-style diet & smoking cessation.
Comorbidities
● 40% of RA deaths are due to CVD.
● Triggers: elevated lipid values, chronic inflammation, 
endothelium dysfunction, & abnormal homocysteine levels.
Medication Management Nursing Responsibilities

Joint Protection & Energy 
Pacing
Activity & Rest Balance: Balance 
scheduled rest periods with daily 
low- impact aerobics and strength 
training.
Adaptive Assistive Devices: Use 
built-up utensils, jar openers, and 
button hooks to preserve function 
and reduce load.
Thermal Modalities: Apply moist 
heat for morning stiffness; utilize 
cold packs during acute 
inflammatory flares.
Nutrition & Holistic Health
Dietary Optimization: Maintain 
target weight to lessen weight 
bearing joint stress; optimize 
protein, iron, and vitamins for 
repair. 
Stress Reduction Techniques: 
Practice guided relaxation and 
deep breathing to mitigate stress-
triggered flares.
Integrative Therapies: 
Acupuncture: may be considered 
as a complementary approach for 
symptom management; verify 
herbs/supplements first.
Psychosocial & Transitional 
Support
Readiness to Learn: Screen and 
address acute pain, fatigue, and 
depressive symptoms prior to 
teaching. 
Life-Stage & Role Concerns: 
Counsel on 
pregnancy/childbearing potential, 
career roles, and family 
responsibilities. 
Resources & Escalation:
Establish provider contact 
thresholds and connect with the 
Arthritis Foundation as well as 
their interdisciplinary team.
Medication & Injection 
Safety
Drug Regimen & Surveillance: 
Teach name, dose, schedule, 
side effects, and routine lab 
monitoring (CBC, LFTs). 
Safe Subcutaneous Self-
Injection: 
Demonstrate sterile technique, 
needle safety, and systematic 
site rotation.
Topical Analgesics Care: 
Apply sparingly to intact skin 
only; avoid eyes/mucosa and 
wash hands post-use.
Patient & Family Education

Medication Management Pain and Joint Management 
Home Safety and Independence
Follow-Up and When to Seek Help
Lifestyle and Health Promotion
Discharge Planning & Home Care
● Take medications as prescribed (e.g., methotrexate, 
hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine).
● Do not stop medications without consulting the 
provider.
● Report medication side effects or signs of infection.
● Use prescribed pain medications appropriately.
● Apply heat to help relieve morning stiffness.
● Balance activity with periods of rest.
● Participate in low-impact exercises to maintain joint 
mobility and strength.
● Use assistive devices recommended by PT/OT 
(e.g., walker, grab bars, adaptive equipment).
● Remove tripping hazards and modify the home 
to reduce fall risk.
● Use energy-conservation techniques to manage 
fatigue.
● Follow an anti-inflammatory diet.
● Maintain a healthy weight.
● Avoid smoking and maintain good 
oral/periodontal hygiene.
● Continue cardiovascular risk reduction and 
bone density care.
● Keep all follow-up appointments with 
rheumatology and primary care.
● Continue laboratory monitoring as 
ordered
● Continue PT/OT as recommended
Report to Your Healthcare Provider
● Worsening joint pain or swelling 
● Fever or signs of infection 
● Unusual fatigue
● New or Concerning symptoms
